blocks.x: Let's see. The first thing I want, since we're interviewing you, we should go first and hear the lady. Could I have your name now?
Loretta Roland Evans.
Roland Golden. Her middle name is the same as yours.
My first husband was Roland and the second one was Evan.
Her first husband was my mother's father.
D-V-A-N-S. Yes. And I'm Dick Allen. I better put that down there.
I thought your name was Dick Lohan.
No. Let's see.
I was thinking of the teenagers at 4 o'clock with my daughter, Dick Lohan. Oh, yeah.
See, the day is August 25th, 1963, Dick. And where are we? What's your address here?

3143, 2 o'clock. Were you born in this neighborhood? No, sir. Where were you born? I was born in New Orleans, but not in this neighborhood. I don't remember. I had to ask. My mother's not here to ask for that. I don't remember.
But where did you grow up? What neighborhood did you grow up in?
I grew up in the Uptown neighborhood. I've always lived Uptown. Around this way, the Garden District, that they call it. I lived out in Chippewater. Used to call that the, what?
Irish Channel?
But I didn't call it the Irish Channel. Out for the St. Thomas Street was Irish Channel.
Further downtown and closer to the river is the Irish Channel.
No, not too far down. It goes down as far, I believe, as out Felicity. I passed that way. Not very far. All out the river, St. Thomas Street, that's what you call Irish Channel.
I hate to ask this question, but do you mind giving the exact date of your birth? You don't have to.

No, I can't say I'm 39. July the 14th, 1891. 1891? I was just figuring up with Yvonne. I was a widow when I was 26. I said, when was that, Yvonne? For goodness sake, Mommy, you forgot the figure. She had to figure it out for me. At 26, I was a widow. That's when I enjoyed my dancing.
Oh, yeah. When you were a widow, you enjoyed your dancing?

Yeah, when I was a teenager, my father was very, very strict. He couldn't. But I loved jazz all the time. But I think there was a lot of ragtime mixed with the jazz. I don't think it was jazz. I think they mixed more ragtime with it.
In those days?
In those days, because we did the turkey trot and the black bottom.
How about the Big Apple?
And the Big Apple, that's something. The Big Apple is formed. That was in 1908, the Big Apple, I think it was. It reminds me of the dance they do at the Golden Age that I belong to now.
Y'all do the Big Apple at the Golden Age?

No, this is something similar to the Big Apple. I don't do it, but I plan on after the, when the winter comes. The Big Apple was something like the square dance. I couldn't think of square dance. So I had to write it down. It was called the classic jitterbug of the swing era in them days. And then we also had the Virginia Reel, an 804 dance, and there was a collar, just like the square dance. But right now, quite a few people can do the square dance, because if you go to the Line Center, they have classes every Wednesday. They're going to start next month again, and I'm going to start taking them dances, because I think it's very good exercise. But we used to do the two-step and the waltz, and in between we'd do the turkey trotting and the ragtime and put a little jazz in it. But nowadays, the youngsters don't want that. They want the steady beat. They want this rock and roll. Even when you go to the cocktail lounges and the casinos, that's all they play there is rock and roll, don't you think so?
Well, it seems to me that most of them are. But do you still have some jazz bands up around this area for neighborhood dancing?

Well, yes, the corner club, any jazz band that you hear is the best jazz band I ever known of was colored jazz bands. They really know how to play. Seven and eight men can play, and you don't need a solace in the jazz band.
You don't need no solace.
Not in the jazz band. I don't think you do.
No.
They can all play at once. They can all play at once.
When did they start having solace? Do you remember that? Did they have them back when you were dancing, in other words?

Yeah, they'd have them every now and then around 19, I think it was around 1910. They used to have solace. When I know, before I married, I married at 20, and we used to dance by the organ grinder then. Not these little organs that they have monkeys on the top. Big organ. And we'd hire an organ, and we'd play outside, and we'd dance in our yard. Bunch of girls and boys. And then when we didn't have the organ, we all played piano. We all knew how to play piano. And we used to play ragtime and jazz, and we'd just shake away. The turkey trot was a shaking dance, you know? It was something similar to what the kids called a jitterbug. They just copied from the old-time dance, that's all I see.
Did you have to make an appointment with this organ grinder, or did you...?

We'd always know how to get him, or we'd know when he was coming in the neighborhood. And we used to have a good time with that organ. And I had a sister that she used to go to Brendan's Pavilion out at Bucktown. They had some jazz bands out there, and blame me, they used to do some. But I couldn't at that time. My father was too strict. I didn't go to too many dances. Just around each girl's house we'd go, and we'd have girls and boys, and we'd all dance. When the sailors come in, we used to be wild about them, same as the girls are now, we'd go out with the sailor boys, and we'd dance.
Well, how is it your sister could go to dances, and you couldn't?

My sister used to sneak off, and come back and talk sweet to my daddy, and never get a weapon, you know, to get out of it. But I was afraid. And the brass band, we had the brass band also, that gave jazz its lusty richness. They used to have that tuber in it, and that bass. I've already seen the three-string bass. They don't have that no more. That's old time.
They were nice, too. I remember those.

They had a rhythm section of drums, all different drums, and then later the piano entered. Now, his mother played in a little band, a bunch of young boys, and she was a pianist. And believe me, they used to put on the music when they played. That's my ring.
I'll stop it.

The pieces, the popular pieces sounded just as fine as the old ones, but they always played with a powerful beat and a variation, you know. Have you ever noticed when, like they're playing on, you're hearing orchestra on television, how they put all that variation on the piano and all. That's not in the piece, but just do that. Have you noticed on Lawrence Waltz, the piano, that girl that plays? She just can put it on. But I don't believe you'd call that ragtime, would you? The way she goes at it. Yeah, you notice her on a Saturday, Lawrence Waltz, that girl that plays the piano. But he has some lovely waltzing on his program. Well, this was before radio time at that time. And that's the time we used to have the phonograph with good records, with the long horn phonographs in those days, you see. We didn't have the phonographs without the horn. They had this long horn. You danced waltzes then? We went to dance waltzes and two steps. Quad wheels and polka. Quad wheel? You never heard of that?
No, what's that?
I don't know, it was some kind of different step. Your mother would know if you'd ask, I bet you. She heard of it.
It's kind of like a square dance in a way, they have a call for that.

I believe the end of ragtime came around 1910. They played ragtime so much and beat it so much that it really ended. And 1917 was when the original jazz band started playing. But I don't know, we didn't seem to like that. I thought it was still ragtime. But everyone said that the jazz age was in the 1920s, and in them days, Armstrong wasn't heard of it. And he really can play jazz. Have you ever heard Louis Armstrong play? Oh, he played.
Yeah, I think we both heard he played a few times.

And I noticed Armstrong say something about Maris, M-A-R-A-S. He played with New Orleans rhythm kings in the 1920s, Maris, Rapola, and Brunis, George Brunis. Did you know those fellas? I heard of them. And I heard him talking about Maris the other night. But I didn't catch if he was still living or where he was or what. He's dead. Yeah, George Brunis later, he joined Ted Lewis's band. Now whether he's still living or not, I don't know.
He asked, we've got an interview with him. Yeah.

But Maris and Rapola. But you couldn't make out much what Armstrong said last night. He reminded me of Louis Frumman who was doing all kinds of humbug. And then we had a lot of small bands. And then it was, the movies were silent up until 1926 when we had talking pictures, I think. It was a year after my last child was born. And Lowest State used to have Waterville and the Sanger. The Dauphine used to have it. The Crescent and Tulane were high class shows. You had to pay more to go there. Palace and then the Dauphine. And after a while the Palace had Burlesque and the Dauphine had Burlesque. Where was the Dauphine? Dauphine's right on the Dauphine Street theater down there from where the Palace is. That's right. The Palace now is a college show. And I remember I used to go to Sangis. I was a great admirer of Louis Primer. And I used to go every week to Sangis. I stayed to see the show twice. I didn't care how good the picture was. But I went more to him and played that trumpet. But believe me, he played. But now when he comes on TV, he does all kinds of humbug.
Singing and talking.
Again. And he don't play like he used to. But in those days, Louis Primer really knew how to play.
Grandma, did, Mother said something the other day about you hiring a band for Edward's birthday.

That was 30 years ago. My daughter and my sister gave a party for my nephew. He was 21. He's 51 now. So that would be about 30 years ago. And my sister didn't remember the band. But I think it was six or an eight piece colored band. And it only cost $2 a man.
That's in 1930.

That was, yeah, that would be around 1930. So they were. Around 1930, that's when the band started getting larger then. But you could get a colored band so cheap then. But they're the ones that really, really played the jazz. And if you hear them at carnival time, they really can play the jazz for you with all these marching clubs. Have you been here for our carnival? Oh, yeah.
Believe me, they played it.
I'm on Boivin Street and on Royal for carnival. I'm here at all.

You never do go along beside the Brex. They don't have women in the corner club or any of those clubs? No, they don't have them. Only men. Only men, yeah. Let's see, what's in the neighborhood here? The buzzards?

The garden? They have some clubs, women, but it would be too expensive for me to join. There's a lot of these night parades of women. Venus is all women and quite a few others. But it's a lot of expensive long times.
Is there any other club down here besides the right now, the Jefferson City Buzzards around here?
Oh, there's a corner club?
The Garden District. The Garden District, yeah.
The Garden District, they're up here and they all play.
The Eleanor, did that go down or not?
No.
They had the Lions and the Eleanor too.

Yeah, they got the Lions and the Eleanor Social Club. Well, they all play, they all have a colored band when you see them. And believe me, they do strut. I mean, strut. It reminds me, years ago when the colored would take their dead, I don't know if they still do it, they'd play when the Saints go marching by and they'd be playing so nice, you know, when they come back. I'll be glad when you rascal you or I'll be glad when you're gone or didn't you ramble when you're coming back to just be jazzing it. Because I've gone to a college funeral just to see what it was all about already. And waited at the cemetery for them and that's how I heard all that. But in 1917, that was the World War. I think that's really when we had jazz. And they had only about five men playing. Then about 1925, we had about seven or eight men started to play. And then I believe that lasted until about 1930 and then the band got up to 12 pieces. And now there's so many bands, I don't know how many pieces the bands have now. Lawrence Walt must have umpteen numbers.
He doesn't play jazz.
Do you remember when the saxophone got popular? Well, I don't know. I think the saxophone and alto, the alto horn is a saxophone also, isn't it? Well, they used to play that in the jazz, alto horn.
That's kind of an upright horn with a mic like a trumpet?

No, it's just like a trumpet, yeah, because my stepson played one. No, it's just a small, like an alto sax, just like that or something. Oh, like this? A lot of the trumpets, yeah. Because my stepson used to play one.
He uses both hands and finger in it.
Yeah.
That's an alto sax. It's got a reed on it like a clarinet.

Yeah, when you play, you play, I think I had something down here about the alto sax. But I really used to like to hear music played. I never did have much of it when I was a young girl. I couldn't do much dancing, but in our houses, in their classical and sentimental music, they played, but jazz was always my favorite.
Well, they played.

Have you noticed now how they're trying to jazz up everything? But why can't they jazz at all? Why did I have to get up? I'm going to the park Sunday again, and I'm going to ask the band leader. And then if you don't do what I ask them, I'll say, you ain't doing that. And Rudy Vallée was on in them days. But he didn't play jazz. He played the sweetest music this side of heaven, soft music. And he's still in existence. He the one people to know how old he is, but Rudy Vallée must be kind of old. I believe in 1934 the radio came out, and then we didn't care so much about the horn. I know when my daughter, Ione was 13, I gave a big party on Broad Street for her. I don't know if we had piano playing, if we had a brass band. I meant to ask her that, a ragtime band. I forgot to ask her when I talked to her the other day.
Did they play music at Wake's drum?
No, only maybe Coler did. I don't know.
Did the white peoples ever have a brass band around here that you saw?
That they'd use for funerals or anything like the Coler did?
Never, it was always a Coler.
I know in olden times, you know, when the president died or some military man, they'd have the military brass band.

Yeah, no, it's only the Coler had a lot of it. I never did have them see the white. You think jazz will ever come back? The kids seem to like the rock and roll and look like they're doing the bop. Oh yeah. You know what you call the bop?
Dancing back and forth. I think it's gonna come back some.

They dance flat-footed. They dance in their bare feet. I think something should be done to educate the public and get them interested in jazz ballroom dancing. I don't expect to do any more of it this late and long, but I think it was beautiful when it lasted. I went to many jazz dancing after I was a widow at 26. But my mother was a great dancer. She used to tell me when she was a girl that she used to run out and dance. And my sister out in Gentilly was another one, and his mother, she danced on the stage, played piano for a band. Of course, she got married at 16 and then she got settled. 17, he was born.
That's your mother played piano.

Yeah, she played piano at 16. She danced on the stage. She was just... She was a swinger. She could dance any kind of dance. She still likes it too. She had to sing to sing to sing to sing to sing to sing to sing to sing to sing to sing to sing to sing to sing to sing to sing to sing to sing to sing to sing to sing to sing to sing to sing to sing to sing to sing to sing to sing to sing to sing to sing to sing to sing to sing to sing to sing to sing to sing to sing to sing to sing to sing to sing to sing to sing to sing to sing to sing to sing to sing to sing to sing to sing to sing to sing to sing to sing to sing to sing to sing to sing to sing to sing to sing to sing to sing to sing to sing to sing to sing to sing to sing to sing to sing to sing to sing to sing to sing to sing to sing to sing to sing to sing to sing to sing to sing to sing to sing to sing to sing to sing to sing to sing to sing to sing to sing to sing to sing to sing to sing to sing to sing to sing to sing to sing to sing to sing to sing to sing to It was close enough to ragtime, but it had in it something of the authentic jazz notes, you know? And I believe they played all through to 1920. But there was a Negro band called King Oliver. I think it was the first Negro jazz band come out. He only had eight pieces. And with or without the second cornet and trumpet, it was considered the perfect makeup in them days for a jazz band. But now it looks like they got to have a tubal. Well, they did have a tubal in them days, too. Now at the Pop Concert, I saw the kettle drum and more instruments and I've seen them since I looked at Lawrence Wells.
Did they have any, what other places did they have here besides West End that they played jazz? How about out on the camps, out on the lake? Did they have bands out there?

Oh, they used to have the old time radios out there with the horns. If they didn't have a band, they would have a radio with a big horn. I mean a phonograph and would have the records. Did you see King Oliver yourself? No, I've heard of him.
He's one of the men you've heard of, right? Yeah.

They had a lot of small bands, but after the, you see they had the Crescent, the Palace, St. Charles, the Dauphine, Lowestate, and the Sanga. Those were all the places where we used to have vaudeville. I don't think it'll ever come back. They had bands with vaudeville. Yeah, they used to have bands with the vaudeville. And the silent pictures that had bands in between, you see. But then the minute the talkies come in, they got rid of the outcastrism. Oh, did you play piano yourself? Yeah, I played years ago. Couldn't play a note now. So I gave my piano to Miss Golden. I don't know what she ever did with me.
She played it for a while, but she finally started.
She played piano too. She danced just for fun on the stage and all, you know. She didn't dance for pay.
Well, what tunes did you play on the piano yourself?

I used to play all these old time songs that I got here. I used to play all these old days. Margie, ain't we got fun? Bye-bye black boy. Waiting for the Robert E. Lee. Let a smile be your umbrella on a rainy day. Don't you hear that sometimes? Yeah, it's new. Sidewalks of New York. And take me back to New York town. New York town, New York town. That's another one.
That's where I long to be. Have you ever heard that one?
No, I haven't heard it. That's a pretty song.

Long so long to me, Coney Island down the bay. And the lights on old Broadway. Here old square, I don't care anywhere. New York town, take me there. Yeah, but there's another song beats it. The romantic city of New Orleans. Way down yonder in New Orleans. That's the first one.
What's that one about the dry? How dry.
And how dry I am. Nobody knows how dry I am. I wish I had a phonograph in the motor records. I'd love to play. I was doing Prohibition. They used to play that.
You didn't have trouble getting a drink though, did you?
No, they used to have that white lightning they sold then. And they used to play the tiger rag. Doesn't they play the tiger rag now?
Yeah.
But they used to rag time at now. But I think now they play the tiger rag and jazz if you ever listen to it on the new clock.
Faster and faster. They're playing that faster and faster. All the time, yeah.

And the Wild Blue Yonder. And the High Society. Valencia. That's another old one. Old Lady Be Goods. And then the Lady in Red. Rum and Coca-Cola. Oh Your Rascal You. The St. Louis Blues. Alexander's Ragtime Band. But that wasn't jazz. It was ragtime. It was called Alexander's Ragtime Band. And it was really ragtime whenever you heard anything about it. When the Saints go marching by, that's so old. I don't know how old that is. They played at all the football games too. And a million dollar baby and a five and ten cents store. And everybody's doing this. Doing what? Turkey truck. See that fella prancing over there? Yeah. I wish I could remember all of them. And Pretty Baby. And yes, oh that's my baby. And then Put Your Arms Around Me Honey Hold Me Tight. Cuddle Up and Cuddle Up With All Your Might. And believe me, when we dance, we cuddle. We didn't do that.
Wasn't any of that arm business.

We win alms. And when you are with two love. That's another one. I wish somebody, a lot of them old pieces are coming back. I sit out on the sidewalk at night and listen to them at the jukebox at the corner. And they're playing so nice and classical and sentimental and all of a sudden you hit them. And I think they're starting to rag to try and do jazz it. But the thing is, they only jazz the chorus. Just like they did Sunday at the park. Now I'm going to pick out a piece Sunday. I don't know what it's going to be, but I'm going to ask Val Valvera. He's a very good musician. He's been one for years. And he knows ragtime. But I went up and asked him. And he said, how did you know? I said, because it's not jazz. What did I want with all them trumpets getting up there? I said, it was jazz. You all would have sat. And played the voice and you'd have played the chorus. They would have, wouldn't they? No, each one got up and played a little bit. I said, I didn't ask to hear each instrument play. I asked you to play me a good jazz number.
You were telling him how to do it. Yeah.
Well, that's the way they did it.

But when you play jazz, you play the whole thing jazz. When Louis Primer got up at the Sanger, and he played a jazz piece, and he was featured with his cornet. He played the first voice and the chorus and everything. And he really knew how to play jazz. If he ever came to Leon Primer's place, I'd like to go see him. And this fella, you know, ought to know how to play jazz. That just come from Lawrence Welp. He doesn't play jazz.
Pete Fountain?
Pete Fountain.
The way he plays jazz is not the old authentic type jazz. When you went to these dances out at Millenburg, how did you get out there?

I didn't go. My sister would go. I didn't know how they went. They went by the old train, Smokey Mary. They used to call the old train out at Millenburg. See that lighthouse at the Spanish Fort? Well, that was formerly Millenburg.
Right out there in the middle of the plate. Yeah. I know where that was.

And that was part of it. But where West End is, is where you call Bucktown. Brendan's Pavilion was in Bucktown, where the Myo Myo Club is. Where I wanted to go for my birthday and you wouldn't take me.
I wonder why.

Well, maybe he doesn't like those drums out there. I went once and I really enjoyed it. She's been trying to get me to go out and take her out there for years. Cute. Another birthday I didn't go. Well, you'd go to Brendan's Pavilion. They had a big pavilion and they had a colored band out there. I don't know. My sister used to sneak and go. I guess she got it from my mother. My mother used to like dancing. Could you spend a weekend out there if you wanted to do? I don't know, but our fathers were too strict to let us spend a weekend.
Where would you catch a train to go out there?

You'd catch a ride up. I don't exactly know where you caught it. But I know it was—they call it the Smokey Mary because they had smoke coming out there. Because I know I've been out there already in that train. And you'd get all full of sut and all riding. It would come in the windows and all. Doesn't look like that out there in the Hallow, does it? I think West End is a beautiful place. I think it's prettier than where Spanish Ford is now. I don't know if they still have a fountain at West End. I used to go to West End to Manasseas when when I was between 19 and 20 and they used to have good music there. But they'd just put on a performance. You couldn't do any dancing then. That was when my first husband was coming to see me. But I had to be home for 10 o'clock, just when the fun would begin. I'd have to be home for nine, but those nights my father would be lenient, let me stay till 10. And the music would just be getting good at 10. And then in between the performance, I'd let you go dance. So it happened that my first husband didn't like dancing, so all I'd do was sit. So his daughter—my daughter sure didn't take after a father because he didn't care for dancing at all. Even the night I got married, he didn't dance. Yeah.
Your mother—your mother danced.
My mother danced.
What tunes did she dance to? Did she ever tell you?

Oh, she danced all those old-time two-steps and I used to hear her say the quadrille and the polka. The golden age, they have a lot of these two-steps and waltzes. And I noticed yesterday at the meeting a lot of them was dancing, so I said, well, I'm going to start catching back the waltzes and two-step. And some of them do that. The bop? The bop. Yeah, you ought to see them people. The old folks do? Yes, indeed. You ought to see them dance. We had a carnival ball. I'm pictured going to be in the carnival balls around the world. Walt Disney took pictures of our ball and I was by the piano singing, somebody love me. And he was all shaking around the piano.
Did you say the captain's 88 years old?

The captain of the crew was 88 years old. We have a man at our club, 88 years old. He dances. I dance with him. You ought to see him dance. They didn't forget it, them old people. They really can can jig around there. They put on some steps. I like it better any day than the dances that they have now. Don't you think so?
Oh yeah. Those are nice dances. I like to hear somebody play Too Much Mustard. Do you remember that?

I've heard of that, yeah. But I haven't heard of it. Too Much Mustard. I only know one fellow that plays it and he stopped playing. You go to Ramport Street, some place there, you can buy all these old-time records. I don't have any more pornograph. I believe my grandson's is broken. And pornograph and radio lately has kind of gotten on my nerves, so I didn't worry about even getting my radio fixed. I can see on the television now, but I don't like it. And you get too much good music on the television to worry about the radio. I go up to the line center sometime and hear them play.
How big was that organ grinder that they grinded to say in comparison to a piano?

Was it big as an upright? It's high like that. It was on a stand. A stand on a big square like that. And it had a hand. A stand on a stand. And that's where he'd grind them. Not as big as a piano. No. Oh no, he used to push it. It had a handle on it like this. And it was high. Three feet high. Yeah, it was a man who would push it, you know. Did he play more than one tune? Oh yeah, we used to pay him. We'd hire him for so many hours. I don't know what we paid him, but we'd hire him for so many hours. And he could change the tune. He could just change the tune one after the other. I don't know how he'd done it. That's one thing I often wanted to find out, but I never did. Someday I will. Often wanted to know how he could change the tune, but I never did go ask him. How about when was that? That was when I was around 18 or 19 years old.
There was a famous guy called Nicodemus was an organ grinder here. I have a little write-up on him somewhere.
You don't see them no more.
I've seen pictures of them.

All you see now is the organ grinder with the monkey, the little organ with the monkey. How about this one? How about this one? How about this one? How about this one? How about this one? How about this one? How about this one? How about this one? How about this one? How about this one? How about this one? How about this one? How about this one? How about this one? How about this one? How about this one? How about this one?
All right, let's see, we were talking about organ grinders. I said they do have one at Cobb's, at the People grind, or a hand organ.

Well, maybe that's what I'm talking about, because they had a hand. But it used to stand, have a stand in the middle. Although it wouldn't have to have a stand, you could put it on a table or a bench or something to stand it up or a prop, however they'd fix it.
Did they have anything else to come to your house or around your house at that time for dances?

That's all I knew we ever had was the organ grinders. We wanted to hire a band, but the banjos have a lot of violin and things like that and more violin and they have cornet. But now they have more trombones and things than they used to have.
Let me think now, what was carnival like in those days when you were young?
I think carnival was the same as it is today. Pretty much the same. Yeah, only we had more masks, more people masks than they do now.
They dress like they do today?
Yeah, dress all different characters. I have a whole book on them. I got scrapbooks on carnival. I cut out all the clippings and put them in my scrapbook.
Where did you used to go to watch parades?

I used to go right on St. Joel Avenue, right out here. Tried to get to Canal Street to be so proud. It was just later I've been going to Canal Street to see it. But I entered the French Quarter. As I found on Royal Street, I could see it without being trampled under, you know? I don't know.
Does it say the carnival was more wild than it is now?
Is it more drinking and carrying on now?
No, I don't think. I don't think they drink any more than they do now. Looks to me as if they drink more now than they did then.
Fight more now than they did then?
Yes, they fight more now than they did then. Boy, people were more peaceful then.
They wouldn't fight at dances in those days or anything like that?
Well, I imagine they did. I didn't go to too many dances to say that. But, um...
Well, did you have open house like some people still do?
Yeah, we always had open house and we played piano. We'd have the radio, the phonograph going. Then after the phonograph left, we had the uh, the radio. The boys are cleaning the grass, I think.
You want to see them? We'll turn it off for a minute. Let me get this one.
It's next to me in the uh, no, this is 58th Carnival. I had some. That one Carnival, I got some in my books, but I didn't know you wanted it.

Well, I just read... Things are written in my books. I got books of it. I'd like to get you to read a poem too a little later, when you feel like reading your favorite poem. But you say the colored people had uh, fish fries? Oh, they always... every Friday night was their fish fries. And where were you living on St. Mary?

I was living... I remember the fish fries on St. Mary. I don't remember them years ago. Well, that was later. That wasn't during the 1920s because my daughters were older than... My daughters were married then when I lived on St. Mary's Street. No, only I own was married. My other two daughters were home.
Did they used to have a fish fry we held at 6th, Grandma? Every Friday? 6th Street, where? Yeah, you know about two blocks somewhere you used to live? Yeah.

Yeah. Yeah, I think there was a fish fry there at the restaurant there. Did they have music that you heard? Oh yeah, they'd have to have music. I don't think the people would come if they didn't have music.
You don't remember what time. What about the shrimp balls and crab balls that the white people had? What did that consist of?
That just would consist of a bunch of people sitting around talking and drinking and eating. Would they have a piano? And they'd have the radio on or something like that. They wouldn't...
Wouldn't have a piano.
They wouldn't worry about getting in a van because they were too busy sitting there eating and drinking to worry about getting up and dancing, you know?
How long would they last?
Oh, they'd last sometimes towards morning.
Do you have a forum about New Orleans? Or is it just a write-up?
Oh, this is just a write-up about it. I wrote this a long time ago. This book is written in there. Dedicated to my daughter Effie. This one's 1935.
Somebody's at the door, Will.

Truly, the old order changes, yielding to the new. So that look where you may in this country, you shall scarcely be able to find a more striking example of this adage than the city of New Orleans affords at its present stage. Here progress is making breaches in the old order, letting in the new. Not since the boom of the thirties, when the city bid fare to rival, if not outshine New York. Has it been seen so much transition? Not in 50 years has there been such a reopening of home pride, civic spirit, and generally among all ranks. New Orleans was founded in 1718 by a French-Canadian, Jean Baptiste, Le Moyne-Circ de Benville. Louisiana was transferred in 1803. 1872 the carnival started. 1918 and 1919 there was no carnival. The war period. 12, 15, 37. We have carnival now for 75 years. 19, 37. I don't know how that sounds.
Why don't you try to read one of your poems if you'd like and run over it once and then we'll do it with a machine on it. 19, 37.
Well, I have a poem I'd like to have published. I don't know if I should put it on it.
Oh, well, oh, well, it's something you've... 19, 38. I have books.
That book was nice. Wait a minute. Let me turn it off. It's ready. Go ahead. Peace.

What is its light if but one day it burns and darkness soon retains? What is its kindness if our face and heart, heart-worn friends depart? What is its plenty if one piteous cry will willfully pass by? What is its music if in the world around we'll let one discard sound? What is thy voice, O Lord, if once we cease to will for earth thy peace? The other one is home. What should be the true meaning of a home? It should be the center where the family may gather into one. Within its walls, love should find a dwelling place. There parents and children should fully share their joys and sorrows. There the great work of training begins. For the duties of the present life and the perfection of another life should begin and be carried on. If not there, where? There the true ends of a human dwelling. This is home. And they were turned down.
Very good. That's very pretty. You've got a lot of talent in writing and everything and you've never had anything published at all?

I just tried. My grandson spurred me on. Not him. I spurred him on for his painting but he never did even take time out to read my portrait. Oh yes, I did. Now, this is one I'm trying to send in and he kind of corrected a little so I'm going to read it according to Rowland's direction. I'm cheerful. It does not cost much to be cheerful nor does it cost much to be sad. No joy will be found if we're tearful. The world has no time to be sad. So let us forgive one another if we have caused sorrow or pain. And think of each one as a brother whose friendship we're trying to gain. Every heart knows much of life's sadness. So give to each one a glad smile and bring in bright rays of gladness. Your own life will then be worthwhile. I'm planning on sending that in. And this is the other one. Today is what you have. It is also what you are and what you do. Today is life. If perchance you have nothing and are nobody and do nothing, Well then for you, there is no today. And this is uh...
This is the one that's your head out of the house, huh?

My little girl. She goes so fast sometimes it seems her baby ways have passed. Though I a baby... Though a baby still I thought I'd a little girl instead. But she could walk and even talk and even fight to have a way. And romp with me upon the floor. But quickly with a pleasure o'er she went to school my precious one. Time swiftly flies. Day is done. Working changes fall my eyes. Which I lift up to the skies. May God guide her long life's way. As she goes from day to day. Tomorrow I shall wait to find a woman grown. This girl of mine. Let's get ready for publication. Now whether they're going to accept this.
I hope they do.
This was written in 1955. To someone I loved very much.

I don't think I can read it right now. All right. We're going to another subject if you don't feel like reading. I was going to ask you do you have any did they have any music in school when you were going to school? Music yes I took music. We used to sing and everything. Music yes. So they had it in the catholic school or public school?

I went to catholic school. I finished. Had eight years grammar school. And three years high school. And I went a year to night school. But there's so many teenagers going there making dates. The teachers didn't have no time for us older folks so I gave up. So it's too late now for me to go take up journalism. And I don't really think I write good enough but I'll take enough journalism if I got to say it myself.
I think it's more of yourself.
And they say I don't write from the heart and from the mind. Gee I think these poems are from my heart and from my mind. I know. And that's my idea of the home room. Is it the recording on there?
Mm-hmm.
And I'm talking.
That's why I was going to ask you about your education what kind of music they taught you know in schools. Did they teach classical music or jazz or religious music?
Well I went to ferocious schools that would be mostly religious.
Mostly religious music that they were teaching. But you did get training on your instrument.

Oh and early up to the fifth grade I went to public school and we was taught other music and other songs you see. When I went to public school we used to go to make down a statue and make fun of day and bring flowers. Up to the fifth grade I went to public and then I left and from then on I went through a parocial. Then I went to Redemptus and finished there. Did you sing when you brought those flowers to the statue? We sang. I used to sing in the choir. I used to like to sing. Next time they have something at the Golden Age I'm going up on stage with them and sing. They wanted me to go last time but I was short of funds and they all had to have a certain costume and I couldn't look as good as they did so that's why I didn't have it. But when you see Walt Disney, the balls is going to come. You see the Golden Age balls and the costume and beautiful. But we had the Nord two weeks ago at the city park and a lady on the next block wanted me to go but I couldn't get a costume. And she has a husband and all and she could buy it and have it made and I didn't have the money to have it done. So I promised her that the next time I have something I'm going to find a way to have a costume. And we sing at the meetings and what's the matter with you? You can sing. Why don't you come with us? So two weeks ago they really sang and they really got clapping. Commissioner Shero congratulated them on the skit they put on. It really was good.
What did you sing when you went up to McDonald's statue?
Oh we'd sing a song that was dedicated to McDonald's. I don't exactly remember. We'd sing that old song Maryland, my Maryland. That used to be a wonder song.
But that was with the McDonald's words. Yeah. That was with McDonald's words. I remember that and I can't remember the words.
Maryland, my Maryland. Oh, John McDonough.
Oh, John McDonough. It goes something like that.
Something like that.
How glorious is our name.

Yeah. We used to sing Stars Bang Havana of course. That's the first song we sang in praise to our flag. We'd all have flowers and every year they still do that. They go off Dr. McDonald's statue. Here's a poem. One I dedicated to my daughter Yvonne. That other one was to my daughter Effie, my little girl. Appreciation. This was written in 1951 I wrote this. And this book has been gone over by a critic. If you see the corrections. Everything's criticized. And told me he's ready for publication. And after that woman done me that I got the cold feet. Because I had no journalism or college. Oh, so much is meant by this void. To said people die of broken hearts. But I do believe it is for lack of appreciation and love. One is usually happy who is appreciated. And the more we appreciate others. The better we feel. I do want you to know I love you. And you appreciate the help, kindness, and happiness you do give me. God bless you and yours. Dedicated to my wonderful daughter Yvonne. This is dedicated to my oldest daughter Ayona. And this was to Ashley again. She was my baby. My baby. A while I held her in my arms. A helpless babe with all her charms. Until she grew so very fast. And baby ways too soon would pass. And when her baby smile had fled. I saw a little girl instead. Who sometimes fought to have her way. And so she grew from day to day. To crown by glorious womanhood. A happy bride before me stood. But timeless miracle had wrought. But I still hold the self-same thought. She's still my laugh and carefully held. And I as always tell myself. She's a baby still to me. And oh I know she'll always be. This is on the poetry exhibits. In 1951 and 1952. And I was also on radio with this poem. And read it. And on the Jackson Square we had this on the fence. This was on the 1951 and 1952. In the French Quarter. On the Jackson Square we had a march up and down. To hear the praise given our. Poetry and this one woman blasted all my hopes. I might have been a great portrait by now. Living in a swell place. This is one that went over big. I thought it did. I wrote this to Roland I believe when he was in the armed forces. A song in everything. There is a song in everything. In every little joy that comes. In babies as they suck their thumbs. The gay notes that the blue voids sing. The mother's patient gentle smile. The glory of the after while. There is no sadness but seems sweet with fragrance. And there is no day but speaks some beauty on life's way. The dusty and the weary feet upon their homeward journey. Bring the lights. The loving hearts may sing. The high chair in the cradle too. Have ever set brave lips to song. No grief has ever lived so long. But turned to music as it grew. And every hour of strife and pain. Leaves in the heart some sweet refrain. Lord teach me this from day to day. To find beyond the heightened care. Thy mercy shining everywhere. That it may brighten life's way. That went over very big.
By the way, did you ever know a fellow named Tom Brown? He lived in this neighborhood. He was a trombone. But I thought you were trying to think of who some of the new-

No, I was living here two years. I lived on the Louisiana Avenue Annunciation before this. I lived on Sixth Street for quite some years. I don't know exactly how long. I lived there, Goodwire on the 16th Constance.
Well, he was a band leader. I thought maybe you'd remember him from there. I haven't danced to his music. Tom Brown or maybe you'd remember Nick Baraka.
He doesn't live too far from there. It seems to me like maybe it was Paul Barbra.
Paul who? Barbra. I doubt it. Probably Nick Baraka up there.

No, I don't remember. And this is dedicated to our eldest son and grandson, Roland. March of Voice, 1955. Our prayers have been for peace and for the safety of our boy. His service in the Navy will very soon be over. Our hearts are filled with joy that he will be home again. And then that he will reach the goal he wants to gain. Wherever he may go in life, we give everlasting thanks. Not just because our boy will be home and he is safe, but for all other blessings, the training and experience to build his confidence and help his character grow. We thank our son and grandson who did the job so well. We thank almighty God and thank the Navy too. What joy is there to quite compare with welcoming our boy. Grandma Loretta, Roland Evans.
Maybe you'd like to hear that.
I don't remember.
You don't remember how much it cost to get in on the dance? Was it expensive in those days? No, it wasn't so very expensive.
Didn't you ever go Dutch treat?
I guess the men always paid, so I can't remember my boyfriend paid.

Well, the men had to pay, of course. We didn't go to Dutch treat. Don't make a sack cheap now. Our men folks in those days, they had to pay the same as they do now. What's it good of having a boyfriend if you can't get them to pay? You mean you only went to a dance so somebody else could pay your way, huh? No, I went to a dance and join myself. Not to dance just with that one fellow if I'd go and want to dance with someone else.
Did you have a lot of boyfriends?

No, I didn't. A lot of different boys. The first boyfriend I had was a man I married. All the other boys didn't mean a thing to me, just dancing. Good times. Where would you go besides dances? It's all to the movies. Then you just have to sit there and look until the talking movies came. Years ago, they wasn't talking. You just have to be written on the screen like they showed last night. Gloria Swanson was showing. Did you see that? Where she was showing private movies? No, I didn't see that. I got a secret. She was showing private movies. She said, don't think I had any part of this. Gloria Swanson, ain't it? She always, as you think she is.
Well, on that band that she's... She's very glamorous. That you hired for $2 East. Didn't you all have them several times after that?

Well, I don't remember if we had them anymore or not after that. We mostly relied on the piano after that and the phonograph. Because everyone played music. And then sometimes I own and her band would come. They'd have a sax in there and a cornet, a drum, a piano. I think they had about a five-piece band. She was a pianist.
That's your daughter and Roland's mother.
Yeah, and she played music. She got married very young at 16.
She must have been pretty talented to have been playing professionally then.
Yeah, she was playing with a band.
Before she was married.

Yeah, and she was on the stage. She went to many benefits at the Jerusalem temple. She didn't perform for money, just at benefits. She'd go. And I'd have to... She'd wear tights and nice costumes. But she was a great dancer. She loved to dance. And then she got married so young. Then she just settled down. No more dancing. But I bet you she can still dance. You can see her dancing around there with a grandchild. I don't think Roland danced as much as his mother. And Donald won in the seminary. He didn't care for it at all.
Well, he didn't get much of a chance at dancing in the seminary.
He didn't. No. He didn't even at home. He didn't care for us at home.
He likes music, though.
But I like good music. I always did. If there's any kind of music on the television, I don't know it's going to be good music. I like to hear it.
Did they have any bands on Bourbon Street then? Or was that where you went to hear some music? Besides the sang?

No, I never knew what it was to go on Bourbon Street. They didn't know much about Bourbon Street then. It used to be called... It was all... Everything was interested in the red light district then on Basin Street. There wasn't so much put on on Bourbon Street in them days.
Uptown people didn't go down that one.
I don't remember going down.
You never went in the French quarters in those days?

Not in them days, no. We didn't go down that way. We were too young to go down in that quarter. It's just the past few years that I've seen much of the French quarter. Well, I worked in the Cabilla and the Presbyter, doing research work, and I learned a lot about the French quarter. I think it's one of the best parts of our city. I think it's lovely. It's like Greenwich Village is to New York. That's their French part in Greenwich Village.
Very pretty buildings and everything.

Yeah, and it's a shame too. Unless they had to repair them, I don't think they should repair them. I'd love to avoid that jazz concert the other night just to hear, really, if they'd have played the whole piece jazz. If you ever hear of any place where they're playing jazz, please let me know. I'd like to go. There's a few left.
You know, Bourbon Street is about all now. It's funny.
I don't think they play jazz on Bourbon Street.
They make too many solos and all that.

Yeah, and they, I know, uh, Carnival Day, I went in more, more of them, they were letting everybody go in, and all they were doing was some kind of swing dancing. I went in the Court of Two Sisters. I went in, I don't know how many nightclubs that were open. All they were doing was swinging back and forth, something similar to what the teenagers are doing. And when I went to the Blue Room two years ago, Sophie Tuckett was there. I went to the Blue Room and they wasn't doing any jazz dancing in the Blue Room at all. They were doing some kind of sophisticated dance. I don't know if it was waltzing or what you call it. And a lot of them was doing this around, like some of the Golden Age do. They go around, the Golden Age can do it too, but I've never tried it. I thought maybe if I'd go on my head if I tried something like that.
Well, uh, I'm surprised though that you didn't go into the French Quarter or any. You didn't go down for coffee and donuts or anything like that.
I went for coffee and donuts, but not when I was young. No, later on I did. When I pass that now, I wish I could go in there and get coffee and donuts, but I just don't go.
Do you remember when the Zulu Parade used to start or didn't it used to start on Bayou St. John?

Uh, the Zulu Parade, I used to go see it. I used to remember when it used to come up the river on a Bayou and they'd get off the float. They'd get off the boat and then have a bunch of the maids waiting for them and the Zulos with the grass, guys dressed just like Zulos and they'd all be jigging and waiting, dancing and there would be a van waiting on the shore for them and they'd all march off. But it was, it was so much nicer and also during Carnival, a long time ago, the Monday of Carnival, I had what you call the king came and Rex came in and he came up the river on a boat. They had out there. How many boats? Just like the Algiers parade they have now on the boats. Yeah. Have you ever gone over to Algiers and see them get off the floats? Mm-hmm. It's beautiful, Carnival Day. I've seen it several times. I had a lady friend who lived over there. Well, the day the king came in, Rex was Tuesday. Well, he came in on Monday at one o'clock and he'd come in by the river and we'd all be lined along waiting for Rex to come off the float. And then, you'd see the king come in and then they'd have a military parade with all soldiers and bands and be beautiful. And then the next day he'd be on the in the Rex parade, but they cut that out. Why? I don't know, but it was really lovely. I've never seen him do that. Huh? I've never seen him do that since I can remember. Well, in my time it was. I don't remember what year, but some of the Carnival organizations would remember. It started in 1872, I believe, Carnival. I said something like that before. Mm-hmm. And that was before my time. But I do remember I used to rush. A bunch of us guys used to rush and see the king come in by the river and we'd be right by the river banks to see him come in. And the Zulu, I used to rush and see him. He came in by Janky's at some time. Ball and Shell's all. Where was Janky's place?
He's got one on Howard Avenue now, but you mean this was on a boat? Came in on a boat. The Zulu came in by Janky's. It's way downtown.

My Effie was a little girl and I had her up on an old oil barrel so she could see the Zulu get off the boat. And I took her that year to see him. It was by Janky's the last time I saw him. So the last few years I didn't have no one to go there and with the situation I didn't want to go by myself. But now they're dressing better than they did years ago. They used to just dress regular Zulu fashion. Now they're putting royal robes and all on now like our floats. I didn't see it last year at all, but the year before last I saw the Zulu. You got to get out for 10 o'clock or I believe he got off the boat before 9 o'clock. But it's beautiful when they get off the boat.
I see it every year. It's nice.

They really have it in Algiers. They have it in Algiers every year, the parade. The parade of Aller, I believe it is. I stood on the river bank and saw them get off the boat and then they go on the float. And then I went and sat right in front of someone's house. They go through all the streets. They don't go just through certain streets like our city. They go through, I don't know how many streets in Algiers. And sat right before this lady's house where all the chairs are and sat there and saw the parade after we saw them get off the boat. But it was so nice to see them coming up the river, you know, and getting off. And all the whistles were blowing and you just knew it was coming. You can hear it over here. Carnival. Is it the day before Carnival? It's the Sunday before Carnival. I have it now. The Sunday before. And you can hear all the whistles.
I was wondering if you remember Happy Shillings Band by any chance?
Shillings Band? I think it was from this neighborhood.
It might well have been.

His mother owned homes where my aunt lived in one of them on Annunciation and what's the street before Louisiana Avenue? Pleasant or Tulledana? Tulledana. Those homes on Pleasant and Tulledana. He really could play Happy Shillings. I think he played jazz quite a bit. And you heard him play? Yeah, he played quite a bit and used to go over to my uncle's that lived right on. He had a big grocery and bar. My mother's brother had a grocery and bar.

segments.title: Opening: names, family and date of recording
segments.summary: Dick Allen introduces the session on August 25, 1963; Loretta gives her name and the two husbands, Roland and Evans, with the grandson present.

segments.title: Birthplace, Uptown childhood and birth date
segments.summary: She was born in New Orleans, grew up Uptown and the Garden District, distinguishes the Irish Channel, and gives her birth date July 14, 1891; widowed at 26.

segments.title: Strict father, turkey trot, black bottom and Big Apple
segments.summary: As a teenager under a strict father she loved jazz mixed with ragtime; dances she did and the Golden Age club dances today.

segments.title: Colored jazz bands, solos and dancing by the organ grinder
segments.summary: She calls colored jazz bands the best; band size, early solos around 1910, and neighborhood dances with a hired organ and piano.

segments.title: Sister at Bucktown pavilion, brass band and her mother-in-law's band
segments.summary: Her sister snuck off to Brendan's Pavilion while she stayed home; the brass band, bass and rhythm section, and a pianist relative.

segments.title: Phonographs, waltzes and quadrilles before radio
segments.summary: She describes long-horn phonographs, waltzing, two-steps, polka and quadrille before radio.

segments.title: End of ragtime, Armstrong, New Orleans Rhythm Kings and the Sanger theater
segments.summary: She dates the end of ragtime and start of jazz band, mentions Armstrong and Brunis, silent movie theaters, and loving Louis Armstrong at the Saenger.

segments.title: Hiring a colored band for $2 a man, c. 1930
segments.summary: A band hired for a nephew's 21st birthday cost two dollars a man; colored bands play jazz at carnival marching clubs.

segments.title: Carnival marching clubs and jazz funerals
segments.summary: Marching clubs, women's night parades, social clubs with colored bands, jazz funeral music, and band sizes from 1917 to 1930.

segments.title: Alto horn, saxophone and her taste in music
segments.summary: Discussion of the alto horn versus saxophone, her stepson's horn, and her lifelong preference for jazz over classical.

segments.title: Rudy Vallee, radio, white brass bands and the future of jazz
segments.summary: Rudy Vallee, radio arriving in 1934, whether white bands played funerals, and whether jazz will return; her dancing mother and daughter.

segments.title: King Oliver, lake camps and vaudeville with bands
segments.summary: King Oliver as first Negro jazz band, jazz at the lake camps by phonograph, and vaudeville houses that had bands before talkies.

segments.title: Playing piano and the old songs she remembers
segments.summary: She names tunes she played and heard, such as Tiger Rag, Alexander's Ragtime Band and When the Saints, and Prohibition-era songs.

segments.title: What real jazz means, versus Pete Fountain and park bands
segments.summary: She argues jazz means playing the whole piece jazz, recalling Louis Armstrong at the Saenger and criticizing the park band and Pete Fountain.

segments.title: Millenburg, Smokey Mary train, West End and courtship
segments.summary: Getting to Millenburg and Bucktown by train, Brendan's Pavilion, and going to West End while courting her first husband.

segments.title: Mother's dances, Golden Age club and old records
segments.summary: Her mother's old dances, Golden Age club dancing, a carnival ball filmed by Walt Disney, and where old records can be bought.

segments.title: The organ grinder at dances
segments.summary: Clarifying how organ grinders worked, how long they were hired, and that they were all they had instead of a band.

segments.title: Carnival in her youth
segments.summary: Carnival then was much like now but with more masks; where she watched parades; whether people drank and fought more.

segments.title: Open house, fish fries and shrimp balls
segments.summary: House parties with piano and phonograph, Friday fish fries with music, and white shrimp and crab ball gatherings.

segments.title: Her writings and poems
segments.summary: She reads a New Orleans write-up and several poems she hopes to publish, with remarks on her schooling and why she gave up night school.

segments.title: School music and singing at the statue; poems for her daughters
segments.summary: Music in public and Catholic school, singing at the statue, her Golden Age singing, and more poems dedicated to daughters.

segments.title: Tom Brown, Nick LaRocca and a poem for her grandson
segments.summary: Dick Allen asks about local bandleaders; she does not recall them and reads a poem for her grandson in the Navy.

segments.chapter: Courtship, family and the French Quarter
segments.title: Paying for dances and boyfriends
segments.summary: Men paid at dances, she danced with many but married her first boyfriend, and movies were the other outing.

segments.chapter: Courtship, family and the French Quarter
segments.title: Daughter Ione's band and her love of dancing
segments.summary: Ione played piano in a five-piece band before marrying at 16; her grandson and Donald and dancing.

segments.chapter: Courtship, family and the French Quarter
segments.title: Bourbon Street, the French Quarter and no real jazz today
segments.summary: She never went to Bourbon Street or the Quarter as a girl, later did research there, and says present-day clubs do not play jazz.

segments.title: Zulu and Rex arriving by boat, carnival in Algiers
segments.summary: Memories of Rex and Zulu arriving by river, taking her daughter Effie to watch, and the Algiers parade.

segments.title: Happy Schilling's band
segments.summary: Asked about Happy Schilling, she places him in the neighborhood and recalls his mother's houses and his playing.
